en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 34 [Tibetan & Sanskrit 37] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[1262'] Now I shall further explain the sequence of rites for the six yoginīs:
one should draw a five-petaled lotus, filled with a pericarp and filaments.
In the center there is Vārāhī, with a red heart and blazing radiance;
she has three faces, six arms, and is gentle;
she has three eyes, her hair is disheveled, she wears a crown of skulls, and she is clad in nothing but space.
Performing dance in the half-lotus posture, their bodies adorned with the six mudrās;
wearing garlands of severed heads, with anklets, they stand upon Kālarātri. All of them trample underfoot the wicked Māra, his enemies, and the [hostile] deities.
Red, blue, and green, adorned with the five mudrās,
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with another hand holding a noose and a goad,
and bearing a severed head, the Goddess who bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
In the heart, one should place the Knowledge Vow (jñānasamaya) born from the union of body, speech, and mind; then,
in a counter-clockwise rotation starting from the east, one should assign the goddesses Yāminī,
Mohinī, Sañcālinī, Santrāsinī, and Caṇḍikā.
She has three eyes and loose, disheveled hair; she is one-faced and four-armed.
She is blue, white, yellow, green, smoky, and grey.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, as well as a bell, a ḍamaru drum, and a curved knife.
Wearing a crown of garlands of skulls and adorned with the five mudrās,
naked and intent on dance, she is decorated with a garland of severed heads;
her crown is bound with Akṣobhya, and she is eager with the essence of the flavor of compassion.
Those who have attained the yoga of non-duality are devoted to Vajrasattva and the others: Vajrasattva is for Vārāhī, Vairocana is prescribed for Yāminī,
Padmanarteśvara for Mohinī, and likewise Heruka for Sañcālī.
In the case of Trāsinī and Vajrasūryā, [the lords are] Caṇḍikā and Paramāśva.
Vajrasattva has a white body; the foremost, Vairocana, is yellow; Padmanarteśvara is red; Heruka is blue; Vajrasūrya is red; and Paramāśva is green.
Alternatively, one should meditate on them individually:
Vajrasattva, with three faces, six arms, and three eyes, adorned with the insignia of the six mudrās;
holding a vajra, [a bell], a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru, and a severed head, dancing, and clothed in human skin.
All the heroes, Vairocana and the others, have one face and four arms, holding a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a ḍamaru drum, and their own respective emblems along with a bell;
or alternatively, one should meditate on them all as having twelve arms and six faces.
Their mantras are as follows:
Oṃ śrī oṃ vaṃ vāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ śrī oṃ haṃ yoṃ yoṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
Oṃ śrī hrīṃ moṃ moṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ śrī hreṃ hrīṃ saṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
Oṃ śrī hūṃ 2 saṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā || Oṃ śrī phaṭ 2 caṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
Thus is the mantra of the six Yoginīs:
Oṃ haṃ vaṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ nama hi bhrūṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ svāhā hūṃ hrīṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vauṣaṭ he heṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho āṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā |
Oṃ phaṭ haṃ hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the mantra of the Six Heroes.
By reciting it while meditating, one accomplishes the supreme sixfold process.
The king attains the status of a universal monarch; there are six such universal monarchs.
One should constantly worship the six symbols— unconquered, completely victorious, and possessed of great strength and prowess— having consecrated them according to the ritual procedure;
thus, for that person, the supreme among the best of king-yogas will be accomplished without long delay.
Having attained perfections such as invisibility and the like, he may roam through the three realms;
as the supreme Vajradhara, he shall ferry sentient beings across the six states of existence within cyclic existence.
Alternatively, one should meditate upon that Great Bliss within hexagonal wheels.
One shall become a sovereign king, a universal monarch (cakravartin) who upholds Mañjuvajra— resembling saffron in hue, blazing with the splendor of divine majesty,
absorbed in the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), and having the nature of the Dharmadhātu.
Embracing from the left and right, he holds a bell and grasps the vajra and breasts;
[he carries] a sword, a book, and a khaṭvāṅga; and in his two hands, a skull-cup, a goad, a lotus, and likewise a hand-drum.

One should place [the syllables] in counter-clockwise order starting from the east: saffron-red, blue, red, green, and white at the top; [these represent] the utterly pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), which liberates the realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu).
The six-limbed heroes joined with the Ḍākinīs;
Vajrasattva with Vārāhī and Vairocana during the watches of the night;
and Padmanarteśvara joined with Mohinī.
Heruka and Sañcālinī, Vajrasūrya and Santrāsinī, as well as Paramāśva and Caṇḍikā—
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one succeeds; Mañjurāṭ himself [is attained].
White, red, yellow, blue, [red], and green; blazing like refined gold and as fair as the sky; green, smoky, and greyish—thus one should visualize the color, with one face and four arms.
The goddesses, however, have two arms and hold a skull-cup and a curved knife;
the heroes carry a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, each joined with their own pair of symbols.
She is joined in union with the bell and holds the supreme *ḍamaru* drum in one hand;
she is three-eyed, stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, and wears a tiger-skin garment. She has a crown of skulls and bears a garland of severed heads.
Visualize her standing upon all the pretas, with Bhairavarātrī in the center;
she has her two knees pressed against the goddess’s [own], with loose hair and naked body.
In her heart is the pledge of gnosis, united with mind, speech, and body.
One should perform the visualization of the two armors and the wheel of the seat;
having placed Vīraḍākinī within the heart of the three secrets,
one should assign Kākāsyā and the others to the Ḍākinīs at the outer gates.
In the corners, one should visualize the Yamadāḍhīs, who are naked;
they possess the colors and insignia previously described, are mounted upon corpses,
stand in the ālīḍha posture, have disheveled hair, and are fierce.
One should meditate upon all those garlanded with skulls, both externally and internally,
through the purification of the six perfections; one should also cultivate that visualization and recite that secret wheel-mantra by means of the yoga of radiating and reabsorbing.
And during the recitations of the heroic yoginīs, one should practice meditative visualization;
the emanation of the assembly of wheels should flash forth, having brought the three worlds to completion.
One should perform the internal meditation and recitation, the secret meditation of the three wheels.
The mantras of the heroes (vīras) are considered to belong to the ḍākinīs and are accompanied by the three principles (tritattva).
During the recitation of mantras containing *hūṃ*, *oṃ*, and *phaṭ*, one should recite those belonging to the three wheels (*tricakrakā*).
Thereafter, the yogin should perform the recitation of the pledge (*samaya*) according to the prescribed rule.
Oṃ śrīmañjuvajra āḥ maṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ haṃ Vajrasattva hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ vāṃ vajravārāhī hūṃ 2 phaṭ [namo] vairocana hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ haṃ yoṃ yoṃ yāminī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ svāhā hūṃ Padmanarteśvara hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
oṃ hrīṃ moṃ [...
oṃ vauṣāṭ[-a] he he ru ka hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
Oṃ hre hrīṃ sañcāraṇī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ hūṃ 2 ho vajrasūrya hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ hūṃ 2 santrāsanī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ phaṭ haṃ Paramāśva hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ phaṭ phaṭ caṇḍikā hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ kākāsye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ ulūkāsye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ svānāsye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śūkarāsye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamadāṭī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamadūtī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamadraṃṣṭrī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ yamamathanī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
One should place the two armors with the left and right hands.
It performs all actions, whatever is desired by the mind.
No doubt should be entertained here; it will certainly succeed, and not otherwise.
Then the Protector, the Lord of the Ten Bhūmis, who is the locus of the ten pāramitās—
The six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom—are the doors to the powers of skillful means, aspiration, and primordial knowledge.
The Joyous, the Stainless, the Luminous, the Radiant, the Difficult to Conquer, the Facing, the Far-Reaching, the Immovable, the Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma—
these one should cultivate through purification.
The four [meditations] beginning with Yamadāḍī are for the purpose of discerning the noble truths.

The Blessed One, the glorious Mañjuvajra, whose very nature is the utterly pure dharmadhātu, has thus taught the instruction for the supreme secret of the most profound *haṭhayoga*, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) consisting of the yoga path of the two-fold pure cultivation—the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—according to its divisions, as the sovereign authority accessible through the Guru. This one should study.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the "Meditation on the Arising of the Yoga of the Two Armors," from the *Abhidhānottara*, the supreme among all tantras, the cause for the means of all vidyās, the great secret, the Heart of the Yoginīs, which bestows the fruits of all rites.
